. Previously, when we studied acid-base reactions in solution, we focused only on the point at which the acid and base were stoichiometrically equivalent, the equivalence point. In this module, we will explore the changes in the concentrations of the acidic and basic species present in a solution throughout the process of a titration and the resulting changes in pH.
Calculations of pH during a titration are different based on the relative amounts of acidic and basic species. There are four phases in the titration to consider.

In the following example, we will calculate the pH throughout a titration between a strong acid and strong base. The pH of a solution of acid or base versus the volume of base or acid added during a titration can be plotted on a graph, known as a titration curve. Take note of the titration curve shown throughout the following example. Later, we will discuss titration curves in more detail.

ions neutralize each other, so only those of the two that were in excess remain, and their concentration determines the pH. Thus, the solution is initially acidic (pH less than 7), but eventually all the hydronium ions present from the original acid are neutralized, and the solution becomes neutral. As more base is added, the solution turns basic.
